prompts: The sky appears blue during the day because molecules in the atmosphere scatter shorter wavelengths of sunlight more strongly than longer ones. This effect, known as Rayleigh scattering, depends on the inverse fourth power of the wavelength, so violet and blue light are scattered many times more than red light. Our eyes are more sensitive to blue than to violet, and some violet light is absorbed high in the atmosphere, which is why the sky looks blue rather than purple. At sunrise and sunset, sunlight travels through a much thicker layer of air before reaching an observer. Most of the blue light is scattered out of the direct path, leaving the reds and oranges that color the horizon. Clouds look white because their water droplets are much larger than the wavelength of visible light, so they scatter all colors almost equally.

Question: A bakery sells muffins for 3 dollars each and cookies for 1 dollar and 50 cents each. On Monday it sold 48 muffins and twice as many cookies. On Tuesday it sold 12 fewer muffins than on Monday but 30 more cookies than on Monday. How much money did the bakery make on the two days combined? Answer: Let us work through the problem step by step. On Monday the bakery sold 48 muffins, which brought in 48 times 3, or 144 dollars. It sold twice as many cookies as muffins, so it sold 96 cookies, which brought in 96 times 1.5, or 144 dollars. On Tuesday it sold 48 minus 12, or 36 muffins, for 108 dollars.

In computer science, a hash table is a data structure that maps keys to values. It uses a hash function to compute an index into an array of buckets, from which the desired value can be found. Ideally, the hash function assigns each key to a unique bucket, but most designs employ an imperfect function, which might cause collisions where the function generates the same index for more than one key. Such collisions are typically handled in some way, for example by chaining entries in a linked list or by probing for another free slot. In a well-dimensioned hash table, the average time complexity for each lookup is independent of the number of elements stored in the table. Many hash table designs also allow arbitrary insertions and deletions of key-value pairs.

Once upon a time, in a small village at the edge of a great forest, there lived an old clockmaker named Elias. Every morning he opened the shutters of his tiny shop and wound each of the hundred clocks that hung on its walls. The villagers said that no two of his clocks ever showed exactly the same time, and yet every one of them was correct in its own way. One winter evening, a young girl knocked on his door, carrying a broken pocket watch that had belonged to her grandfather. She asked whether he could make it run again. Elias turned the watch over in his hands, opened its back, and looked for a long time at the tiny gears inside.

Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants, algae, and some bacteria convert light energy into chemical energy. During the light-dependent reactions, which take place in the thylakoid membranes of chloroplasts, chlorophyll absorbs light and uses its energy to split water molecules, releasing oxygen as a by-product. The energy captured in this stage is stored temporarily in the molecules ATP and NADPH. In the second stage, the Calvin cycle, which occurs in the stroma, the plant uses ATP and NADPH to fix carbon dioxide from the air into three-carbon sugars. These sugars can then be assembled into glucose, starch, cellulose, and many other organic compounds that the plant needs to grow.

Question: A train leaves a station at 9:00 in the morning traveling at 60 kilometers per hour. A second train leaves the same station on the same track at 10:30 traveling at 90 kilometers per hour in the same direction. At what time will the second train catch up with the first, and how far from the station will they be? Answer: When the second train departs, the first train has already been traveling for one and a half hours, so it is 60 times 1.5, or 90 kilometers ahead. The second train gains on the first at a rate of 90 minus 60, which is 30 kilometers per hour. To close a gap of 90 kilometers at 30 kilometers per hour takes 3 hours.

The history of the printing press begins in the fifteenth century, when Johannes Gutenberg developed a system of movable metal type in the German city of Mainz. Earlier printing methods in East Asia had used carved wooden blocks and, later, movable type made of ceramic or metal, but Gutenberg combined several innovations: an alloy of lead, tin, and antimony that could be cast precisely, an oil-based ink that adhered well to metal, and a screw press adapted from those used to make wine. The result was a process that could produce books far more quickly and cheaply than hand copying. Within a few decades, printing shops had spread to more than two hundred cities across Europe.

To make a simple tomato sauce, start by heating two tablespoons of olive oil in a heavy pan over medium heat. Add one finely chopped onion and cook it slowly, stirring from time to time, until it becomes soft and translucent, which usually takes about eight to ten minutes. Add two cloves of minced garlic and cook for another minute, taking care not to let the garlic brown. Pour in a can of whole peeled tomatoes and crush them with the back of a wooden spoon. Season with salt, a pinch of sugar, and a few leaves of fresh basil. Let the sauce simmer gently for twenty to thirty minutes, until it has thickened and the oil begins to separate at the edges.
